ety.text: From Middle English egge, from Old English eċġ, from Proto-West Germanic *aggju, from Proto-Germanic *agjō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”). See also Dutch egge, German Ecke, Danish æg, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish egg; also Welsh hogi (“to sharpen, hone”), Latin aciēs (“sharp”), acus (“needle”), Latvian ašs, ass (“sharp”), Ancient Greek ἀκίς (akís, “needle”), ἀκμή (akmḗ, “point”), and Persian آس (âs, “grinding stone”)).

senses.d: The boundary line of a surface.
A one-dimensional face of a polytope. In particular, the joining line between two vertices of a polygon; the place where two faces of a polyhedron meet.
An advantage.
ex: I have the edge on him.

senses.d: The thin cutting side of the blade of an instrument, such as an ax, knife, sword, or scythe; that which cuts as an edge does, or wounds deeply, etc.
ex: Speaking with a metallic edge to her voice.
There was an unmistakable edge to her remarks.

senses.d: A sharp terminating border; a margin; a brink; an extreme verge.
ex: The cup is right on the edge of the table.
He is standing on the edge of a precipice.

senses.d: Sharpness; readiness or fitness to cut; keenness; intenseness of desire.
ex: After the timeout there was a new edge to the team's play.
Death and persecution lose all the ill that they can have, if we do not set an edge upon them by our fears and by our vices.

senses.d: The border or part adjacent to the line of division; the beginning or early part (of a period of time)
ex: supposing that the new general, unacquainted with his army, and on the edge of winter, would not hastily oppose them.

senses.d: A shot where the ball comes off the edge of the bat, often unintentionally.
ex:
2004 March 29, R. Bharat Rao Short report: Ind-Pak T1D2 Session 1 in rec.sports.cricket, Usenet
Finally another edge for 4, this time dropped by the keeper

senses.d: A connected pair of vertices in a graph.
A level of sexual arousal that is maintained just short of reaching the point of inevitability, or climax.
To move an object slowly and carefully in a particular direction.
ex: He edged the book across the table.
The muggers edged her into an alley and demanded money.

senses.d: To move slowly and carefully in a particular direction.
To win by a small margin.
To hit the ball with an edge of the bat, causing a fine deflection.
To trim the margin of a lawn where the grass meets the sidewalk, usually with an electric or gas-powered lawn edger.
To furnish with an edge; to construct an edging.
To furnish with an edge, as a tool or weapon; to sharpen.
To form a border to; to enclose, to border.
To make sharp or keen; to incite; to exasperate; to goad; to urge or egg on.
ex: By such reasonings, the simple were blinded, and the malicious edged.

senses.d: To intentionally stay or keep someone extremely close to the point of orgasm for a long period of time.
ex: Jimmy has been edging for 6 hours straight; is his dick okay?
